claim: Laser-capture microdissection (LCM) and RNA-seq were applied to characterize the intestinal transcriptome of Schmidtea mediterranea.
source: Here, we applied laser-capture microdissection (LCM) and RNA-seq to characterize the intestinal transcriptome of Schmidtea mediterranea, a planarian flatworm that can regenerate all organs, including the gut.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the methods used in the study.

claim: Hundreds of genes with intestinal expression were identified that were undetected by previous approaches.
source: We identified hundreds of genes with intestinal expression undetected by previous approaches.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study.

claim: Extensive conservation of digestive physiology and cell types exists between planarians and other animals, including humans.
source: Systematic analyses revealed extensive conservation of digestive physiology and cell types with other animals, including humans.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a result of systematic analyses.

claim: Previously unappreciated regionalization of gene expression exists in the planarian intestine along the medio-lateral axis, especially among intestinal goblet cells.
source: Furthermore, spatial LCM enabled us to uncover previously unappreciated regionalization of gene expression in the planarian intestine along the medio-lateral axis, especially among intestinal goblet cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this discovery from spatial LCM.

claim: Two intestine-enriched transcription factors specifically regulate regeneration (hedgehog signaling effector gli-1) or maintenance (RREB2) of goblet cells.
source: Finally, we identified two intestine-enriched transcription factors that specifically regulate regeneration (hedgehog signaling effector gli-1) or maintenance (RREB2) of goblet cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the identification and functional roles of these transcription factors.

claim: Physical trauma, disease, and aging can damage the digestive tract, causing numerous human gastrointestinal pathologies.
source: Physical trauma, disease, and aging can damage the digestive tract, causing numerous human gastrointestinal (GI) pathologies (Li and Jasper, 2016; Andersson-Rolf et al., 2017; Peery et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice and Drosophila can repair damage to the digestive epithelium.
source: Mice and Drosophila can repair damage to the digestive epithelium, and recent studies have elucidated cellular and molecular mechanisms underpinning these abilities (Gehart and Clevers, 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; Zwick et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Some animals can repair or completely replace severely damaged or missing gastrointestinal tissue.
source: Some animals are endowed with much greater regenerative capacity, and can repair or even completely replace severely damaged or missing GI tissue (Goodchild, 1956; O'Steen, 1958; Takeo et al., 2008 ; Kaneko et al., 2010; Zattara and Bely, 2011; Mashanov et al., 2014; Okano et al., 2015), but the underlying mechanisms are far less understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Schmidtea mediterranea has become a powerful model for addressing the molecular and cellular underpinnings of organ regeneration.
source: Driven by the recent application of genomic and molecular methods, the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea has become a powerful model in which to address the molecular and cellular underpinnings of organ regeneration (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002; Robb et al., 2015; Brandl et al., 2016; Grohme et al., 2018; Reddien, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts proliferate and differentiate in response to surgical amputation injury in planarians.
source: In response to nearly any type of surgical amputation injury, pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts proliferate and differentiate, regenerating brain, intestine, and other tissues lost to injury (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Rink, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pre-existing tissue undergoes extensive remodeling and re-scaling through collective migration of post-mitotic cells and proportional loss of cells through apoptosis in planarians.
source: In addition, pre-existing tissue undergoes extensive remodeling and re-scaling through both collective migration of post-mitotic cells in undamaged tissues, as well as proportional loss of cells through apoptosis (Pellettieri, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Re-establishment of proportion, symmetry, and function of planarian organ systems occurs within a few weeks after injury.
source: These processes are coordinated to achieve re-establishment of proportion, symmetry, and function of planarian organ systems within a few weeks after injury (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The planarian intestine has a highly branched morphology with a single anterior and two posterior primary intestinal branches.
source: In uninjured planarians, a single anterior and two posterior primary intestinal branches project into the head and tail, respectively, with secondary, tertiary, and quaternary branches extending toward lateral body margins (Hyman, 1951; Forsthoefel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Growth and regeneration of intestinal branches require considerable remodeling of pre-existing tissue.
source: Growth and regeneration of intestinal branches require considerable remodeling of pre-existing tissue (Forsthoefel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Remodeling of planarian intestinal tissue is governed by axial polarity cues, ERK and EGFR signaling pathways, cytoskeletal regulators, and interactions with muscle.
source: Remodeling is governed by axial polarity cues (Pellettieri, 2019; Forsthoefel and Newmark, 2009), extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling pathways (Umesono et al., 2013; Hosoda et al., 2016; Barberán et al., 2016), cytoskeletal regulators (Forsthoefel et al., 2012), and interactions with muscle (Adler and Sánchez Alvarado, 2017; Seebeck et al., 2017; Bonar and Petersen, 2017; Scimone et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: New intestinal cells differentiate at the severed ends of injured gut branches and in regions of significant remodeling.
source: New intestinal cells (the progeny of neoblasts) differentiate at the severed ends of injured gut branches, as well as in regions of significant remodeling, providing an intriguing example of how differentiation and remodeling must be coordinated to achieve integration of old and new tissue (Forsthoefel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Three cell types comprise the planarian intestinal epithelium: secretory goblet cells, absorptive phagocytes, and outer intestinal cells.
source: Only three cell types comprise the intestinal epithelium: secretory goblet cells, absorptive phagocytes (Willier et al., 1925; Ishii, 1965; Bowen et al., 1974), and a recently identified population of basally located 'outer' intestinal cells (Fincher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transcription factors expressed by intestinal progenitors and their progeny have been identified.
source: Transcription factors expressed by intestinal progenitors ('gamma' neoblasts) and their progeny have been identified (Forsthoefel et al., 2012; Fincher et al., 2018; Wagner et al., 2011; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Labbé et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The EGF receptor egfr-1 is required for integration of intestinal cells into gut branches.
source: However, only the EGF receptor egfr-1 (Barberán et al., 2016) has been shown definitively to be required for integration of intestinal cells into gut branches, and therefore the functional requirements for differentiation of new intestinal cells are largely undefined.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of intestine-enriched transcription factors nkx2.2 and gata4/5/6-1 causes reduced blastema formation and/or decreased neoblast proliferation.
source: Knockdown of several intestine-enriched transcription factors (nkx2.2, gata4/5/6-1) causes reduced blastema formation and/or decreased neoblast proliferation (Forsthoefel et al., 2012; Flores et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of the intestine-enriched HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase wwp1 causes disruption of intestinal integrity, reduced blastema formation, and neoblast loss.
source: Similarly, knockdown of the intestine-enriched HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase wwp1 causes disruption of intestinal integrity, reduced blastema formation, and neoblast loss (Henderson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of egfr-1 causes hyperproliferation and expansion of several neoblast subclasses.
source: Conversely, knockdown of egfr-1 causes hyperproliferation and expansion of several neoblast subclasses (Barberán et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A method for purifying intestinal phagocytes from single-cell suspensions derived from planarians fed magnetic beads was previously developed.
source: Previously, we developed a method for purifying intestinal phagocytes from single-cell suspensions derived from planarians fed magnetic beads, enabling characterization of gene expression by this cell type (Forsthoefel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Single-cell profiling of whole planarians has distinguished individual intestinal cell types and transitional markers for neoblasts differentiating along endodermal lineages.
source: More recently, single-cell profiling of whole planarians has distinguished individual intestinal cell types, as well as transitional markers for neoblasts differentiating along endodermal lineages (Fincher et al., 2018; Labbé et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Laser-capture microdissection was developed as a precise method for obtaining enriched or pure cell populations from tissue samples.
source: Laser-capture microdissection (LCM) was developed as a precise method for obtaining enriched or pure cell populations from tissue samples, including archived biopsy and surgical specimens (Emmert-Buck et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LCM has been used to address a vast array of basic and clinical problems requiring genome, transcriptome, or proteome analysis in specific tissues or cell types.
source: Since its introduction, LCM has been used to address a vast array of basic and clinical problems requiring genome, transcriptome, or proteome analysis in specific tissues or cell types (Mahalingam, 2018; Bevilacqua and Ducos, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LCM requires sample preparation including fixation, histological sectioning, and tissue labeling or staining.
source: LCM requires sample preparation including fixation, histological sectioning, and tissue labeling or staining (Espina et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: For expression profiling using LCM, tissue processing must be optimized to maintain morphology and labeling of cells of interest, as well as RNA integrity.
source: For subsequent expression profiling, tissue processing must be optimized to maintain morphology and labeling of cells of interest, as well as RNA integrity (Espina et al., 2006; Goldsworthy et al., 1999; Gillespie et al., 2002; Golubeva and Warner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Appropriate tissue-processing conditions for extraction of intact RNA from planarian tissue sections were identified.
source: We first identified appropriate tissue-processing conditions for extraction of intact RNA from planarian tissue sections.
evidence: The abstract states this as a methodological achievement.

claim: The planarian intestinal transcriptome was characterized using RNA-Seq, bioinformatics approaches, and whole-mount in situ hybridization.
source: Then, using RNA-Seq, bioinformatics approaches, and whole-mount in situ hybridization, we characterized the intestinal transcriptome.
evidence: The abstract states the methods used to characterize the transcriptome.

claim: Previously unappreciated regionalization and diversity of intestinal cell types and subtypes were discovered, especially amongst goblet cells.
source: We discovered previously unappreciated regionalization and diversity of intestinal cell types and subtypes, especially amongst goblet cells, and hundreds of intestine-enriched transcripts not identified in recent single-cell profiling efforts.
evidence: The abstract states this as a discovery from the study.

claim: 22 intestine-enriched transcription factors were identified, including several required for production and/or maintenance of goblet cells.
source: In addition, we identified 22 intestine-enriched transcription factors, including several required for production and/or maintenance of goblet cells, setting the stage for further studies of this cell type.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study.

claim: Methacarn fixation enabled better RNA recovery than formaldehyde fixation.
source: None of the relaxation treatments detrimentally affected RNA quality, but methacarn (a precipitating fixative) enabled much better RNA recovery than formaldehyde (a cross-linking fixative) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B as supporting data.

claim: Eosin Y alone or with Hematoxylin enabled superior demarcation of the intestine compared to Hematoxylin alone.
source: For all three mucus-removal methods, Eosin Y alone or with Hematoxylin enabled superior demarcation of the intestine, as compared to Hematoxylin alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1C as supporting data.

claim: Magnesium relaxation was superior for preservation of morphology compared to NAc and HCl treatment.
source: For preservation of morphology, magnesium relaxation was superior; NAc and HCl treatment caused tearing and detachment of intestine from the slide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1C as supporting data.

claim: Prominent 18S/28S rRNA peaks indicated that the combination of magnesium-induced relaxation, brief methacarn fixation, and rapid Eosin Y staining were suitable for LCM and extraction of RNA of sufficient quality for RNA-Seq.
source: Although additional freezing, cryosectioning, staining, and drying steps required for LCM caused a modest decrease in RNA integrity relative to whole animals (compare Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with 1D), prominent 18S/28S rRNA peaks (which co-migrate in planarians, as in some other invertebrates [Ishikawa, 1977; Matz, 2002; Winnebeck et al., 2010; Asai et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D]) indicated that the combination of magnesium-induced relaxation, brief methacarn fixation, and rapid Eosin Y staining were suitable for LCM and extraction of RNA of sufficient quality for RNA-Seq.
evidence: The text states this conclusion based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and cites supporting literature.

claim: 13,136 of 28,069 transcripts in the reference transcriptome were detected in non-intestine, medial intestine, and/or lateral intestine.
source: Altogether, we detected 13,136 of 28,069 transcripts in the reference transcriptome (46.8% coverage) in non-intestine, medial intestine, and/or lateral intestine (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1C as supporting data.

claim: 1844 transcripts were upregulated in either medial or lateral intestine, or both.
source: Of these, 1844 were upregulated in either medial or lateral intestine, or both (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1C as supporting data.

claim: 1748 transcripts were significantly upregulated in medial intestine compared to non-intestine.
source: Specifically, in medial intestine, 1748 transcripts were significantly upregulated (fold-change >2 and FDR-adjusted p-value<0.01) compared to non-intestine (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1D as supporting data.

claim: 1627 transcripts were upregulated in lateral intestine.
source: In lateral intestine, 1627 transcripts were upregulated (Figure 1D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1D as supporting data.

claim: 1,531 of 1,844 transcripts were upregulated in both medial and lateral intestine.
source: Although most (1,531/1,844) transcripts were upregulated in both medial and lateral intestine, a small subset of transcripts was significantly upregulated only in medial (217/1,844) or lateral (96/1,844) intestine (Figure 1D), relative to non-intestine.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1D as supporting data.

claim: 143 of 162 transcripts tested by WISH had detectable expression in the intestine.
source: 143/162 transcripts (~88%) had detectable expression in the intestine (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text states this validation result and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1 as supporting data.

claim: Most transcripts were expressed uniformly throughout the intestine.
source: Most transcripts were expressed uniformly throughout the intestine (e.g. ATPase H+-transporting accessory protein 2 (atp6ap2), cytochrome P450 2B19 (cyp2b19), cytochrome P450 2A6 (cyp2a6), and prosaposin (psap); Figure 1F, blue borders, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this observation and references Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data.

claim: Transcripts predicted by RNA-Seq to be most enriched in medial intestine branches were indeed expressed at higher levels in these regions.
source: By contrast, transcripts predicted by RNA-Seq to be most enriched (>1.5X) in medial intestine branches (e.g. carboxypeptidase A2 (cpa2), rapunzel 4 (rpz4), and gastric triacylglycerol lipase (lipf), green borders, Figure 1F) or lateral intestine branches (e.g. a carboxypeptidase homolog (ct14378), serine peptidase inhibitor Kunitz type 3 (spint3), and a novel gene ('novel'), orange borders, Figure 1F) were indeed expressed at higher levels in these regions.
evidence: The text states this validation result and references Figure 1F as supporting data.

claim: Anteriorly and posteriorly enriched transcripts were discovered.
source: Additionally, although we did not explicitly compare anterior and posterior gene expression, we also discovered anteriorly (a C-type lectin (Zgc:171670/dd_79), Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and posteriorly (lysosomal acid lipase (lipa/dd_122), Figure 1—figure supplement 2) enriched transcripts, consistent with the influence of anteroposterior polarity cues on intestinal morphology (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008; Reuter et al., 2015; Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015; Stückemann et al., 2017).
evidence: The text states this discovery and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cites supporting literature.

claim: 900 of 1,317 transcripts were significantly upregulated in both phagocytes and laser-microdissected intestine.
source: 900/1,317 transcripts were significantly upregulated in both phagocytes and laser-microdissected intestine (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2A as supporting data.

claim: 74 of 82 transcripts upregulated in both phagocytes and laser-microdissected intestine displayed uniform, ubiquitous expression throughout the intestine.
source: As expected, the majority (74/82) of these transcripts, which included previously identified intestinal markers hnf-4 and nkx2.2 (Wagner et al., 2011; Forsthoefel et al., 2012; Garcia-Fernàndez et al., 1993), displayed uniform, ubiquitous expression throughout the intestine, consistent with enrichment in phagocytes (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: 358 intestine-enriched transcripts were not significantly up- or down-regulated in phagocytes.
source: 358 intestine-enriched transcripts were not significantly up- or down-regulated in phagocytes (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1 as supporting data.

claim: Some transcripts not significantly up- or down-regulated in phagocytes were enriched in goblet cells.
source: However, others were expressed in a distinct subset of less abundant intestinal cells (peptidase inhibitor 16 (pi16) and serine peptidase inhibitor, Kunitz type 3 (spint3), Figure 2D). These transcripts are enriched in goblet cells, since their WISH expression pattern is highly similar to labeling of this subpopulation by lectins (Zayas et al., 2010), antibodies (Ross et al., 2015; Reuter et al., 2015; Bueno et al., 1997), and other recently identified transcripts (Fincher et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018; Reuter et al., 2015).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2D and cites supporting literature.

claim: Some transcripts not significantly up- or down-regulated in phagocytes were enriched in basal regions of the intestine.
source: A third set of transcripts was enriched in basal regions of the intestine (zgc:172053, a homolog of human C-type lectin collectin-10, and calmodulin-3 (calm3), Figure 2D). This pattern resembles that of a planarian gli-family transcription factor (Rink et al., 2009) and several solute carrier-family transporters (Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015), and indicates expression by 'outer intestinal cells' (which we refer to as 'basal cells' because of their proximity to the basal region of phagocytes) that were also recently identified in a large-scale, single-cell sequencing effort (Fincher et al., 2018).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2D and cites supporting literature.

claim: 59 intestine-enriched transcripts were significantly downregulated in phagocytes.
source: Finally, 59 intestine-enriched transcripts were significantly downregulated in phagocytes (Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1 as supporting data.

claim: Transcripts significantly downregulated in phagocytes were enriched only in goblet cells or basal cells.
source: As expected, we never observed uniform, phagocyte-like expression patterns for these transcripts (Figure 2F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Rather, transcripts in this group were enriched only in goblet cells (e.g. epididymal secretory protein E1/Niemann-Pick disease type C2 protein (npc2)) or basal cells (e.g. solute carrier family 22 member 6 (slc22a6)).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data.

claim: Some goblet-cell-specific transcripts appeared to be either medially or laterally enriched.
source: Furthermore, some goblet-cell-specific transcripts also appeared to be either medially (e.g. metalloendopeptidase (cg7631)) or laterally (e.g.,eppin) enriched (Figure 2F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting possible specialization of this cell type along the mediolateral axis.
evidence: The text states this observation and references Figure 2F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data.

claim: 91 transcripts with a ubiquitous intestinal expression pattern were identified by WISH, and nearly all were upregulated in sorted phagocyte data.
source: Overall, validation by WISH identified 91 transcripts with a ubiquitous intestinal expression pattern; nearly all of these were upregulated in our sorted phagocyte data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A as supporting data.

claim: 25 validated goblet-cell-enriched transcripts and 25 basal-cell-enriched transcripts were identified, most of which were not upregulated in sorted phagocytes.
source: By contrast, most of the 25 validated goblet-cell-enriched transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and 25 basal-cell-enriched transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) were not upregulated in sorted phagocytes.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C as supporting data.

claim: Expression of cathepsin La (ctsla) was ubiquitous throughout intestinal branches but did not overlap with npc2 or slc22a6.
source: Expression of the most phagocyte-enriched transcript, cathepsin La (ctsla), was ubiquitous throughout intestinal branches, but did not overlap with npc2, a goblet-cell-enriched mRNA (Figure 3A), or with slc22a6, a basally enriched transcript (Figure 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3A and Figure 3B as supporting data.

claim: Goblet cell-enriched npc2 was expressed by cells with minimal slc22a6 expression.
source: Goblet cell-enriched npc2 was expressed by cells with minimal slc22a6 expression (Figure 3C), further reinforcing that npc2+ goblet cells are distinct from ctsla+ phagocytes as well as slc22a6+ basal cells.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3C as supporting data.

claim: slc22a6+ basal cells were distinct from visceral muscle fibers that surround intestinal branches.
source: We also found that slc22a6+ basal cells were distinct from visceral muscle fibers that surround intestinal branches, occupying basal regions around digestive cells (Kobayashi et al., 1998; Orii et al., 2002), consistent with another study (Scimone et al., 2018; Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 3D–E and cites supporting literature.

claim: slc22a6+ cells represent a novel cell type in the intestine that is distinct from visceral muscles, phagocytes, and goblet cells.
source: Thus, slc22a6+ cells represent a novel cell type in the intestine that is distinct from visceral muscles, phagocytes, and goblet cells, and that has, to our knowledge, not been described by numerous previous histological and ultrastructural studies. Our data independently confirm the identification of this cell type in a recent single-cell sequencing effort (Fincher et al., 2018).
evidence: The text states this conclusion based on the data presented and cites supporting literature.

claim: A subpopulation of goblet cells restricted to medial regions of the intestine, mainly localized to primary branches, was identified.
source: These included a subpopulation of goblet cells restricted to medial regions of the intestine, mainly localized to primary branches (Figure 4A and C), and a lateral subpopulation within secondary, tertiary, and quaternary branches (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 4A and C as supporting data.

claim: A lateral subpopulation of goblet cells within secondary, tertiary, and quaternary branches was identified.
source: These included a subpopulation of goblet cells restricted to medial regions of the intestine, mainly localized to primary branches (Figure 4A and C), and a lateral subpopulation within secondary, tertiary, and quaternary branches (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 4B–C as supporting data.

claim: Goblet cells in medial and lateral domains only rarely co-mingled or co-expressed both markers at the mediolateral boundaries between primary and secondary branches.
source: Only rarely did goblet cells in these medial and lateral domains co-mingle, or co-express both markers at the mediolateral boundaries between primary and secondary branches (Figure 4C).
evidence: The text states this observation and references Figure 4C as supporting data.

claim: Subpopulations of basal cells in lateral regions of the intestine were identified.
source: We also identified subpopulations of basal cells in lateral regions of the intestine (Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B as supporting data.

claim: Transcripts expressed by multiple cell types in different combinations and levels were identified.
source: Finally, we also identified transcripts expressed by multiple cell types in different combinations and levels (Figure 4E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), illustrating the complexity of gene expression even in a tissue with relatively few cell types.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 4E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D as supporting data.

claim: There was considerable agreement between verified in situ expression patterns and cell-type enrichment predicted by scRNA-Seq studies.
source: There was considerable agreement between our verified in situ expression patterns and cell-type enrichment predicted by scRNA-Seq studies, although we did identify numerous additional cell-type-specific transcripts (Figure 5A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 5A as supporting data.

claim: Phagocyte-, goblet-, and basal-cell-specific transcripts from scRNA-Seq studies mapped to similar quadrants in phagocyte vs. laser-captured intestine plots.
source: In addition, phagocyte-, goblet-, and basal-cell-specific transcripts from scRNA-Seq studies mapped to similar quadrants in our phagocyte vs. laser-captured intestine plots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–H as supporting data.

claim: The majority of phagocyte-enriched transcripts detected in an earlier study were also enriched in laser-captured intestine.
source: Similarly, the majority of phagocyte-enriched transcripts detected in our earlier study (Forsthoefel et al., 2012) were also enriched in laser-captured intestine (Figure 5B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 5B and cites supporting literature.

claim: 809 intestine-enriched transcripts were identified that single-cell studies did not find to be enriched in the intestine.
source: Furthermore, we identified 809 intestine-enriched transcripts that single-cell studies did not find to be enriched in the intestine (or for some, any planarian cell type) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 5C as supporting data.

claim: 22 of 28 transcripts identified exclusively by LCM-RNA-Seq were validated by WISH to be intestine-enriched.
source: Using WISH, we validated intestine enrichment for 22/28 of these mRNAs (Figure 5D–H), including transcripts with a uniform/phagocyte-like expression pattern (Figure 5D), and others with expression in goblet and basal cells (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: The text states this validation result and references Figure 5D–H as supporting data.

claim: Over 1000 intestine-enriched transcripts in scRNA-Seq studies were not included in the LCM-generated transcriptome.
source: We also note that over 1000 intestine-enriched transcripts in scRNA-Seq studies were not included in our LCM-generated transcriptome (Figure 5C).
evidence: The text states this observation and references Figure 5C as supporting data.

claim: The vast majority (>80%) of intestine-enriched transcripts in scRNA-Seq studies not included in the LCM transcriptome were enriched in multiple cell types.
source: However, the vast majority (>80%) of these were enriched in multiple cell types (Fincher et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018; Supplementary file 2), suggesting considerable expression in non-intestinal tissue, consistent with our data.
evidence: The text states this observation and cites supporting literature.

claim: Expression profiling of laser-captured bulk tissue may be more sensitive than current single-cell profiling approaches for detecting tissue-specific gene expression.
source: However, the detection of transcripts exclusively enriched in laser-captured intestine suggests that expression profiling of laser-captured bulk tissue is more sensitive than current single-cell profiling approaches, and that LCM may be a preferable method for assessing tissue-specific gene expression when single-cell resolution is not required.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: Metabolic processes were among the most highly represented Gene Ontology Biological Process terms among intestine-enriched transcripts.
source: Metabolic processes were among the most highly represented: hundreds of transcripts were predicted to regulate catabolism, biosynthesis, and transport of a variety of macromolecules (e.g. lipids and carbohydrates) and small molecules (e.g. amino acids and ions) (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding based on Gene Ontology analysis.

claim: Hundreds of upregulated transcripts were predicted to regulate molecular transport, vesicular trafficking, and organelle-based import and export.
source: Hundreds of upregulated transcripts were also predicted to regulate molecular transport, vesicular trafficking, and organelle-based import and export (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A as supporting data.

claim: Over 70 members of the solute carrier family of transmembrane transporters were identified among upregulated transcripts.
source: These included over 70 members of the solute carrier family of transmembrane transporters (Supplementary file 3B), reinforcing the intestine's central role in metabolite transport, and also suggesting a potential role supporting the excretory system in maintaining extracellular solute concentration (Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015; Andrikou et al., 2019).
evidence: The text states this finding and cites supporting literature.

claim: Nearly 30 Ras-related Rab GTPase proteins were identified among enriched regulators of vesicular trafficking.
source: Enriched regulators of vesicular trafficking also included nearly 30 Ras-related Rab GTPase proteins (Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The text states this finding.

claim: Transcripts predicted to coordinate phagosome, endosome, and lysosome physiology were among the most highly represented among regulators of organelle and cellular physiology.
source: Among regulators of organelle and cellular physiology, transcripts predicted to coordinate phagosome, endosome, and lysosome physiology were among the most highly represented (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding.

claim: Several vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein (vps) homologs required for lysosome tethering to late endosomes and autophagosomes were identified.
source: These included several vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein (vps) homologs required for lysosome tethering to late endosomes and autophagosomes (Spang, 2016), and homologs of the autophagy-related proteins atg3 and atg7, ubiquitin ligases that are required for autophagosome formation during nutrient starvation (Komatsu et al., 2005; Sou et al., 2008), and which may contribute to planarians' ability to survive extended fasting (Felix et al., 2019).
evidence: The text states this finding and cites supporting literature.

claim: Many intestine-enriched genes were predicted to regulate cell shape, motility, polarity, and adhesion.
source: As in our previous study of phagocyte expression (Forsthoefel et al., 2012), here we also identified many intestine-enriched genes predicted to regulate cell shape, motility, polarity, and adhesion, including numerous cytoskeletal regulators, regulators of interactions with extracellular matrix, and partitioning defective 6 (pard6b), which we previously demonstrated was required for planarian intestinal remodeling (Forsthoefel et al., 2012; Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding and cites supporting literature.

claim: Transcripts predicted to regulate responses to stress, microorganisms, and other stimuli were intestine enriched.
source: Finally, transcripts predicted to regulate responses to stress, microorganisms, and other stimuli were also intestine enriched (Figure 6).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6 as supporting data.

claim: Over 30 tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor homologs (TRAFs) were identified among regulators of innate immunity.
source: Prominent among these were regulators of innate immunity, including over 30 tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor homologs (TRAFs), a family of adaptor proteins that is expanded in S. mediterranea (Swapna et al., 2018) and function as effectors of receptor signaling in innate and adaptive immunity (Xie, 2013; Arnold et al., 2016; Supplementary file 3D).
evidence: The text states this finding and cites supporting literature.

claim: 62 intestine-enriched transcripts were previously found to be upregulated in response to shifting planarians from recirculating to static culture conditions.
source: Notably, 62 intestine-enriched transcripts (from this study) were previously found to be upregulated in response to shifting planarians from recirculating to static culture conditions, which causes microbiome dysbiosis (Arnold et al., 2016; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6—source data 2A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Figure 6—source data 2A, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Homologs of 99 S. mediterranea intestine-enriched transcripts were upregulated by ingestion of pathogenic bacteria in Dugesia japonica.
source: Further supporting a role for the intestine in innate immunity and/or inflammatory responses, homologs of 99 S. mediterranea intestine-enriched transcripts were also upregulated by ingestion of pathogenic bacteria in Dugesia japonica, a related planarian species (Abnave et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 6—source data 2B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and Figure 6—source data 2B, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Most functional categories predicted by LCM transcript analysis were also enriched among phagocyte scRNA-Seq transcripts.
source: Most functional categories predicted by LCM transcript analysis (Figure 6) were also enriched among phagocyte scRNA-Seq transcripts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Figure 6—source data 1B–D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A as supporting data.

claim: GO analysis suggested that basal cells may play a significant role in metabolism and energy processing.
source: Furthermore, GO analysis suggested that basal cells may play a significant role in metabolism and energy processing, and that goblet cells may influence extracellular matrix organization and play specialized roles in lipid metabolism (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Figure 6—source data 1B–D).
evidence: The text states this inference based on GO analysis and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2A as supporting data.

claim: GO analysis suggested that goblet cells may influence extracellular matrix organization and play specialized roles in lipid metabolism.
source: Furthermore, GO analysis suggested that basal cells may play a significant role in metabolism and energy processing, and that goblet cells may influence extracellular matrix organization and play specialized roles in lipid metabolism (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and Figure 6—source data 1B–D).
evidence: The text states this inference based on GO analysis and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2A as supporting data.

claim: Analysis of biological process GO term enrichment among medial transcripts identified numerous putative regulators of innate immunity and macromolecular catabolism.
source: Analysis of biological process GO term enrichment among all 1221 medial and 623 lateral transcripts – without regard to cell-type specificity – identified numerous putative regulators of innate immunity and macromolecular catabolism among medial transcripts, and of extracellular matrix organization among lateral transcripts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D and Figure 6—source data 1E–H).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D as supporting data.

claim: Analysis of biological process GO term enrichment among lateral transcripts identified numerous putative regulators of extracellular matrix organization.
source: Analysis of biological process GO term enrichment among all 1221 medial and 623 lateral transcripts – without regard to cell-type specificity – identified numerous putative regulators of innate immunity and macromolecular catabolism among medial transcripts, and of extracellular matrix organization among lateral transcripts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D and Figure 6—source data 1E–H).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D as supporting data.

claim: Many transcripts with the greatest medial or lateral enrichment in the intestine were expressed by goblet cells.
source: Intriguingly, many transcripts with the greatest medial (97) or lateral (56) enrichment (e.g. >1.5X in medial vs. lateral tissue or vice versa) in the intestine were expressed by goblet cells (Figure 2C–F, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 2C–F, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data.

claim: GO analysis of the most medially and laterally enriched transcripts suggested possible functional specialization of goblet cells with respect to lipid metabolism, protein processing, extracellular matrix organization, and innate immunity.
source: GO analysis of these transcripts suggested possible functional specialization with respect to lipid metabolism, protein processing, extracellular matrix organization, and innate immunity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E and Figure 6—source data 1I–J).
evidence: The text states this inference based on GO analysis and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2E as supporting data.

claim: Goblet cells express pancreatic carboxypeptidase A2 and lipase F/gastric triacylglycerol lipase, which are predicted to be secreted regulators of protein and triglyceride catabolism.
source: For example, in support of previous suggestions that goblet cells promote luminal digestion (Arnold, 1909; Pedersen, 1961; Jennings, 1962), we identified several goblet-enriched transcripts predicted to encode secreted regulators of protein catabolism (pancreatic carboxypeptidase A2) and triglyceride catabolism (lipase F/gastric triacylglycerol lipase) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Three goblet-enriched kallikreins were identified.
source: Second, we also identified three goblet-enriched kallikreins (klk) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), secreted proteases whose mammalian homologs produce vasoactive plasma kinin, but also hydrolyze extracellular matrix molecules, growth factors, hormone proteins, and antimicrobial peptides in numerous tissues (Prassas et al., 2015).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Kallikreins are expressed by goblet cells in rat, cat, and mouse intestines.
source: Kallikreins are expressed by goblet cells in rat, cat, and mouse intestines (Schachter et al., 1986; Grün et al., 2016), and have been implicated in inflammatory bowel disease and gastrointestinal cancers (Stadnicki, 2011; Kontos et al., 2013), suggesting additional conservation of planarian goblet cell physiology.
evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claim: Goblet cells express peptidoglycan recognition protein (pgrp-1b).
source: Third, goblet cells express peptidoglycan recognition protein (pgrp-1b) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), whose vertebrate and invertebrate homologs modulate innate immune signaling and play direct bactericidal roles (Kurata, 2014; Dziarski and Gupta, 2018), suggesting goblet cells may coordinate immune responses and/or regulate microbiome composition.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: A homolog of prohormone convertase (pcsk1) is enriched in goblet cells and peripharyngeal cells.
source: Fourth, a homolog of prohormone convertase (pcsk1) is enriched in goblet cells, as well as peripharyngeal cells surrounding the pharynx (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3C as supporting data.

claim: Prohormone convertases (PCs) cleave neuropeptide and peptide hormone preproteins to generate bioactive peptides.
source: Prohormone convertases (PCs) cleave neuropeptide and peptide hormone preproteins to generate bioactive peptides.
evidence: The text states this as established knowledge.

claim: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, PCs function in neurons and in endocrine cell types such as pancreatic islet cells and digestive tract enteroendocrine cells, where they regulate glucose levels, energy homeostasis, and appetite.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, PCs function in neurons, but also in endocrine cell types such as pancreatic islet cells and digestive tract enteroendocrine cells, where they regulate glucose levels, energy homeostasis, and appetite (Grün et al., 2016; Pauls et al., 2014; Stijnen et al., 2016).
evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claim: pcsk1 expression suggests goblet cells may play an enteroendocrine-like role.
source: Although another planarian pcsk paralog, Smed-pc2, processes neuropeptides required for germline development (Collins et al., 2010), to our knowledge, no intestine-enriched prohormones have been reported. Nonetheless, pcsk1 expression suggests goblet cells may play an enteroendocrine-like role, as in other organisms.
evidence: The text states this inference based on pcsk1 expression and cites supporting literature.

claim: Genes encoding planarian homologs of gel-forming mucins were expressed by peripharyngeal cells that send projections into the pharynx, not by goblet cells.
source: Finally, we were surprised to find that genes encoding planarian homologs of gel-forming mucins (which we identified in separate bioinformatic searches) were expressed not by goblet cells, but by peripharyngeal cells that send projections into the pharynx (Forsthoefel et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3D as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Some planarian gel-forming mucin proteins may be delivered to the intestinal lumen through the pharynx.
source: While additional goblet-enriched proteins with mucin-like roles might exist (Bocchinfuso et al., 2012; Syed et al., 2008), these expression patterns suggest that some planarian gel-forming mucin proteins are delivered to the intestinal lumen through the pharynx, and indicate a possible difference between planarian and vertebrate intestinal goblet cells (Birchenough et al., 2015; Chang et al., 1994; Johansson et al., 2011).
evidence: The text states this inference based on expression patterns and cites supporting literature.

claim: The intestine expresses numerous homologs of transcripts that are enriched in human GI tissues.
source: Further illustrating the conservation of physiological roles, we found that the intestine expresses numerous homologs of transcripts that are enriched in human GI tissues (Figure 7A–E, Supplementary file 4, and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7A–E, Supplementary file 4, and Figure 7—source data 1 as supporting data.

claim: 5583 planarian transcripts encoding predicted ORFs have high homology to ORFs in UniProt human transcripts.
source: To make this comparison, we conducted reciprocal best homology (RBH) searches (Bork et al., 1998; Tatusov et al., 1997) to identify 5583 planarian transcripts encoding predicted open reading frames (ORFs) with high homology to ORFs in UniProt human transcripts (The UniProt Consortium, 2018), and vice versa (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7A–B as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Four of the five tissues to which the planarian intestine was most similar are involved in digestion or energy storage/metabolism.
source: Strikingly, four of the five tissues to which the planarian intestine was most similar are involved in digestion (duodenum, small intestine, and gallbladder) or energy storage/metabolism (liver) (Figure 7E).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7E as supporting data.

claim: The planarian intestine was also similar to other human digestive tissues (esophagus, colon, and rectum), as well as kidney.
source: The intestine was also similar to other human digestive tissues (esophagus, colon, and rectum), as well as kidney, possibly suggesting a role supporting the planarian protonephridial system in filtration or processing of extracellular solutes (Figure 7E; Thi-Kim Vu et al., 2015; Rink et al., 2011; Scimone et al., 2011).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 7E as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: Duodenum- and small intestine-enriched RBH transcripts included predicted regulators of endodermal specification, bile transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose transport.
source: Duodenum- and small intestine-enriched RBH transcripts included predicted regulators of endodermal specification, bile transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose transport (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The text states this finding.

claim: RBH homologs enriched in liver included several predicted regulators of glucose, amino acid, lipid, and xenobiotic compound metabolism.
source: In addition, RBH homologs enriched in liver included several predicted regulators of glucose, amino acid, lipid, and xenobiotic compound metabolism (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The text states this finding.

claim: Physiological roles performed by multiple human digestive organs are consolidated in the planarian intestine.
source: These observations reinforce the evolutionary conservation of intestinal gene expression and indicate that physiological roles performed by multiple human digestive organs are consolidated in the planarian intestine.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: Knockdown of gli-1 dramatically reduced goblet cells at the midline in regenerating intestine in tail fragments.
source: Knockdown of a second transcription factor, gli-1 (a transducer of hedgehog signaling [Rink et al., 2009; Glazer et al., 2010]), caused failure of goblet cells to regenerate at the midline of the new anterior branch in amputated tail fragments regenerating a new head (Figure 8A–B, Supplementary file 5C, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B, Supplementary file 5C, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: In gli-1(RNAi) animals, goblet cells were less abundant in pre-existing regions of the intestine, particularly in lateral intestinal branches.
source: In addition, goblet cells were less abundant in pre-existing regions of the intestine, particularly in lateral intestinal branches (Figure 8A–B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: Regeneration of goblet cells was reduced in new tail branches of gli-1(RNAi) head fragments and in anterior and posterior branches in gli-1(RNAi) trunk fragments.
source: Regeneration of goblet cells was also reduced in new tail branches of gli-1(RNAi) head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) and in anterior and posterior branches in gli-1(RNAi) trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 2B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C as supporting data.

claim: Effects of gli-1 knockdown on goblet cells were specific, since phagocytes and basal cells regenerated normally.
source: These effects on goblet cells were specific, since phagocytes (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C) and basal cells (Figure 8B) regenerated normally.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A, Figure 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cells appeared to differentiate normally in regenerating intestine, including at the midline of anterior intestinal branches in tail fragments.
source: By contrast to the gli-1 phenotype, goblet cells appeared to differentiate normally in regenerating intestine upon knockdown of a third TF, ras-responsive element binding protein 2 (RREB2), including at the midline of anterior intestinal branches in tail fragments (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), in posterior branches in head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), and in both anterior and posterior branches in trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, new goblet cells were largely restricted to the midline/primary branches in tail and trunk regenerates.
source: However, in tail and trunk regenerates, new goblet cells were largely restricted to the midline/primary branches (Figure 8A–B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and C), and were less abundant in posterior branches of head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell numbers were dramatically reduced or completely absent in pre-existing intestinal regions, especially lateral branches.
source: Furthermore, in pre-existing intestinal regions (especially lateral branches), goblet cell numbers were dramatically reduced or even completely absent. These included the posterior of tail fragments (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), the anterior of head fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), and central regions of trunk fragments (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) animals, phagocytes and basal cells were unaffected.
source: As with gli-1, phagocytes and basal cells were unaffected (Figure 8A–B; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C as supporting data.

claim: gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches.
source: Together, these results suggest that gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches, while RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
source: Together, these results suggest that gli-1 regulates neoblast fate specification and/or differentiation of neoblast progeny into goblet cells in new intestinal branches, while RREB2 may control maintenance or survival of goblet cells after they initially differentiate.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: In uninjured animals, gli-1 knockdown reduced goblet cell numbers, especially in anterior, posterior, and lateral intestine branches.
source: Knockdown of gli-1 reduced goblet cell numbers in uninjured animals, especially in anterior, posterior, and lateral intestine branches (Figure 8C), but many goblet cells remained in medial, primary intestinal branches.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8C as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, goblet cells were more dramatically reduced in all regions of the intestine.
source: In RREB2(RNAi) animals, goblet cells were more dramatically reduced in all regions of the intestine (Figure 8C).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8C as supporting data.

claim: In gli-1(RNAi) uninjured animals, almost no lateral goblet cells remained, while medial goblet cells were much less affected.
source: Indeed, we found (using additional goblet cell markers) that almost no lateral goblet cells remained in gli-1(RNAi) uninjured animals, while again, medial goblet cells were much less affected (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3A as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, reduction of both medial and lateral goblet cell numbers was pronounced, but some lateral goblet cells remained.
source: By contrast, in RREB2(RNAi) uninjured animals, reduction of both medial and lateral goblet cell numbers was pronounced, but nonetheless some lateral goblet cells remained (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3A as supporting data.

claim: In gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates, both medial and lateral goblet cell subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch.
source: For example, both subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch in gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B), and both subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches of RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3B as supporting data.

claim: In RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates, both medial and lateral goblet cell subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches.
source: For example, both subpopulations failed to differentiate in the primary anterior intestinal branch in gli-1(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B), and both subpopulations were severely reduced in pre-existing, posterior branches of RREB2(RNAi) tail regenerates (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 3B as supporting data.

claim: In uninjured animals undergoing normal homeostatic growth and renewal, gli-1 is primarily required for differentiation of new lateral intestinal cells.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that, in uninjured animals undergoing normal homeostatic growth and renewal, gli-1 is primarily required for differentiation of new lateral intestinal cells.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: RREB2 is required for maintenance of both medial and lateral goblet cells, although lateral cell numbers are slightly less affected by RREB2 knockdown compared to gli-1.
source: Conversely, RREB2 seems to be required for maintenance of both medial and lateral goblet cells, although lateral cell numbers are slightly less affected by RREB2 knockdown, compared to gli-1.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: Mechanisms regulating goblet cell differentiation and maintenance may differ during homeostasis and regeneration.
source: These complex observations suggest that mechanisms regulating goblet cell differentiation and maintenance may differ during homeostasis and regeneration, or that compensatory mechanisms capable of sustaining goblet cell production/survival in uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals are insufficient to meet the increased demand for new tissue during regeneration.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: gli-1 mRNA is most highly enriched in phagocytes, basal cells, and intestine-associated muscle cells (visceral muscle), but is also expressed at lower levels in some goblet cells.
source: In fact, gli-1, which was previously shown to be expressed by intestine-associated cells (Rink et al., 2009; Currie et al., 2016), was most highly enriched in phagocytes, basal cells, and intestine-associated muscle cells (visceral muscle), but was also expressed at lower levels in some goblet cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 4A as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: RREB2 mRNA is enriched in goblet cells and basal cells, but expression was also observed in some phagocytes and intestine-associated muscle.
source: RREB2 was enriched in goblet cells and basal cells, but expression was also observed in some phagocytes and intestine-associated muscle (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 4B as supporting data.

claim: Knockdown of fer1 (PTF1A) and lhx2b modestly reduced goblet cells in pre-existing branches.
source: Intriguingly, we found that knockdown of two other TFs, 48 related 1 (fer1) (also called pancreas transcription factor one subunit alpha or PTF1A [Fincher et al., 2018]), and LIM homeobox 2 (lhx2b), also modestly reduced goblet cells in pre-existing branches (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–C and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 5A–C and Supplementary file 5 as supporting data, and cites supporting literature.

claim: mRNAs encoding fer1 (PTF1A) and lhx2b are enriched in basal regions of the intestine.
source: mRNAs encoding these TFs are enriched in basal regions of the intestine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 6—figure supplement 1 as supporting data.

claim: Single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage.
source: In addition, single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage (Fincher et al., 2018), and PTF1A also reduces basal intestinal cell numbers (Fincher et al., 2018).
evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claim: PTF1A reduces basal intestinal cell numbers.
source: In addition, single-cell transcriptome data suggest PTF1A expression is elevated in differentiating neoblast progeny in the basal cell lineage (Fincher et al., 2018), and PTF1A also reduces basal intestinal cell numbers (Fincher et al., 2018).
evidence: The text states this claim and cites supporting literature.

claim: Basal cells (and possibly phagocytes or muscle cells) may non-autonomously influence goblet cell differentiation and/or survival.
source: Thus, although our data support a role for gli-1 and RREB2 in goblet cells and/or their precursors, they also raise the possibility that basal cells (and possibly phagocytes or muscle cells) may non-autonomously influence goblet cell differentiation and/or survival.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: Some uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) planarians refused food and failed to eat after 4–5 weeks of dsRNA feeding.
source: Over a 6 week dsRNA feeding regimen, some uninjured gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) planarians refused food and failed to eat after 4–5 weeks (Figure 8D).
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8D as supporting data.

claim: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died.
source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died (Figure 8—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that goblet cells are required for viability.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6A as supporting data.

claim: Goblet cells are required for viability.
source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) animals, some animals eventually lysed, curled, or died (Figure 8—figure supplement 6A), suggesting that goblet cells are required for viability.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6A as supporting data.

claim: A modest (but insignificant) decrease in animal size was observed in RREB2(RNAi) planarians relative to controls.
source: Additionally, we observed a modest (but insignificant) decrease in animal size (Figure 8—figure supplement 6B–C) in RREB2(RNAi) planarians relative to controls.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8—figure supplement 6B–C as supporting data.

claim: Feeding failure and other phenotypes were only observed in animals fed dsRNA 1x/week for 6 weeks, not in animals fed 2x/week for six times.
source: Interestingly, we only observed feeding failure and other phenotypes in animals fed the dsRNA/liver mix 1x/week (every 7 days) for 6 weeks; animals that were fed 2x/week (every 3–4 days), but still six times, did not refuse to eat, lyse, curl, or die (not shown).
evidence: The text states this observation.

claim: Goblet cells may regulate hunger (or other aspects of digestive physiology) primarily in starved animals.
source: This suggests that goblet cells may regulate hunger (or other aspects of digestive physiology) primarily in starved animals, consistent with expression of prohormone convertase (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), above.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3C as supporting data.

claim: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell depletion was robust, but neither gene was required more generally for regeneration.
source: In both gli-1(RNAi) and RREB2(RNAi) regenerates, goblet cell depletion was robust (Figure 8A–B), but neither gene was required more generally for regeneration (with the infrequent exception of reduced posterior blastemas in gli-1(RNAi) regenerates, mentioned above), as the brain (Figure 8E), pharynx (Figure 8E), other intestinal cell types (Figure 8A–B), and new intestinal branches (Figure 8A–B) all regenerated without noticeable defects.
evidence: The text states this finding and references Figure 8A–B and Figure 8E as supporting data.

claim: Goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration.
source: Together, these results suggest that goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration, and that their primary role may be to regulate appetite or other aspects of intestinal physiology that contribute to viability.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.

claim: The primary role of goblet cells may be to regulate appetite or other aspects of intestinal physiology that contribute to viability.
source: Together, these results suggest that goblet cells are broadly dispensable for regeneration, and that their primary role may be to regulate appetite or other aspects of intestinal physiology that contribute to viability.
evidence: The text states this inference based on the data presented.
